title: Define, Implement, and Validate Mitigations
intro: Closing the loop from finding to fix: choosing targeted mitigations such as adversarial training, provenance tracking, data validation and injection-resistant design patterns; applying filtering, sandboxing, rate limiting and watermarking well; prioritising mitigations by risk reduction, feasibility and business context; validating fixes with regression testing; and monitoring the residual risk that remains.
objectives: Select targeted mitigations for specific AI attack classes, including adversarial training, provenance tracking, data validation and isolation patterns
Apply filtering, sandboxing, rate limiting and watermarking, and tune them against both missed attacks and false positives
Prioritise mitigations by risk reduction, feasibility and business context, using interim controls and recorded risk treatment
Validate mitigations with regression suites that test variants and utility, behind release gates
Monitor residual risk with key risk indicators, scheduled testing, canaries and reassessment triggers
Compare empirical and certified robustness, and select and evaluate guardrail models as one layer of defence

blocks.title: Matching the fix to the attack

scenes.title: Matching the fix to the attack
scenes.say: A finding is only useful if it leads to the right fix. Generic controls help, but each class of AI attack has mitigations aimed at its root cause, and each has costs and limits. | This video covers targeted mitigations, including adversarial training, provenance tracking, data validation and design patterns that contain prompt injection.

scenes.title: Attack class and targeted mitigation
rows: Costs accuracy; new attacks still work
Subtle poisons can pass the checks
Safety training; input and output classifiers
Slows attackers rather than stopping them
scenes.say: Each attack class has its own targeted mitigations, and each has limits. | Evasion: adversarial training, which adds attack examples to training, and preprocessing of inputs. Both cost some accuracy, and new attacks still work. | Poisoning: validating data and tracking its provenance, so only checked data from known sources reaches training. Subtle poisons can still pass the checks. | Prompt injection: design patterns that isolate untrusted content, and least-privilege tools. These limit what the system can do, and may need a redesign. | Jailbreaks: safety training, plus classifiers on inputs and outputs. These add cost and some over-refusal. | And extraction: rate limits, returning only what users need, and monitoring for probing. These slow attackers down rather than stopping them.

scenes.title: Design patterns that contain injection

items.d: Acts, but never reads tool output
Tracked data flow in a safe language
Drop what later steps don’t need

scenes.say: Prompt injection can’t be filtered away reliably, so a 2025 paper by researchers from several companies and universities set out design patterns that contain it. The principle: once an agent has read untrusted input, that input must not be able to trigger consequential actions. | Action-selector: the agent can trigger actions, but never reads their output. | Plan-then-execute: the plan of tool calls is fixed before any untrusted content is read. | Map-reduce: each untrusted item is processed by an isolated worker, and only constrained results are combined. | Dual LLM: a privileged model coordinates, while a quarantined model handles untrusted text and returns only placeholders. | Code-then-execute: a privileged model writes a program in a restricted language, so the flow of tainted data can be tracked and checked. | And context minimisation: remove content that later steps don’t need, so it can’t influence them.

scenes.def: Anthropic’s Constitutional Classifiers (2025): 0.38% more refusals and about 24% more compute.
scenes.ex: A public challenge still found one universal jailbreak.
scenes.say: Here is what a well-targeted mitigation can achieve. In 2025, Anthropic tested input and output classifiers trained against jailbreaks. Automated jailbreak success fell from eighty-six per cent to four point four per cent. | The cost was a small rise in refusals, about four tenths of a per cent, and about a quarter more compute. | And in a public challenge, one participant still found a universal jailbreak. Targeted mitigations reduce risk substantially, but rarely remove it, which is why they are layered and monitored.

items: Match each mitigation to the attack’s root cause
Validate data and track provenance against poisoning
Contain prompt injection by design, not just filters
Every mitigation has costs and limits: layer and measure
scenes.say: To recap. | Match each mitigation to the root cause of the attack it addresses. | Validate data and track its provenance to defend against poisoning. | Contain prompt injection by design, rather than relying on filters alone. | And remember that every mitigation has costs and limits, so layer them, and measure what they achieve.

blocks.md:
### Choosing targeted mitigations
| Threat | Targeted mitigations | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Evasion** | Adversarial training; input transformation; ensembles; certified robustness for some models | Robustness to known attacks often costs accuracy (Module 6.1) |
| **Poisoning and backdoors** | Trusted, signed sources; provenance tracking; validation and quarantine; deduplication and outlier checks; backdoor scanning and testing | Combine with evaluation after training (Modules 3.3 and 6.3) |
| **Prompt injection** | Isolation design patterns; least-privilege tools; human approval for consequential actions; output validation | Filters help, but aren’t sufficient on their own |
| **Jailbreaks** | Safety training on red-team data; input and output classifiers; monitoring | Expect a trade-off with over-refusal |
| **Extraction and inversion** | Authentication, rate limits and quotas; returning only needed detail (no raw scores); differential privacy; watermarks for ownership evidence | Raises attackers’ costs (Module 3.6) |
| **Data leakage** | Data minimisation; permission-aware retrieval; DLP on outputs | Treat outputs as untrusted (Module 3.5) |

### Adversarial training
Adversarial training adds attack examples, with correct labels or safe responses, to training or fine-tuning, so the model learns to resist them. For language models, the equivalent is **safety fine-tuning on red-team data**, often paired with **classifiers** on inputs and outputs. Know its limits: it hardens the model against the attacks it has seen, new techniques can still succeed, it can reduce accuracy or helpfulness, and it needs repeating as attackers adapt. Validate it with held-out attacks, not the training examples (Section 4).

### Provenance tracking and data validation
- **Provenance tracking:** record where every dataset, document and model came from, with hashes, signatures and lineage, so only approved inputs reach training and retrieval, and a poisoned source can be traced and removed (Module 6.3).
- **Data validation gates:** schema and format checks, value ranges, label consistency, duplicate and outlier detection, and scanning for personal data and toxic or injected content, with suspicious items quarantined for review (Module 3.3).
- **Approved snapshots:** train only on versioned, validated and signed snapshots.

### Containing prompt injection by design
Module 4.4 introduced plan-then-execute and privileged and quarantined models. The 2025 paper *Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections*, by researchers from organisations including IBM, Invariant Labs, ETH Zurich, Google and Microsoft, describes six patterns: **action-selector**, **plan-then-execute**, **LLM map-reduce**, **dual LLM**, **code-then-execute** and **context minimisation**. Google DeepMind’s research system **CaMeL** (2025) applies the same idea, separating control flow from data flow and attaching capabilities to data, so untrusted content can’t change what the agent does. Each pattern gives up some flexibility for security; choose by the agent’s risk tier.

blocks.title: Which mitigation targets the threat?
pairs: A competitor queries an API at scale to copy the model
Rate limits, quotas and output minimisation
Scraped web pages may contain planted training samples
Provenance tracking and data validation gates
An email agent might act on instructions in incoming mail
Plan-then-execute, with approval for actions
A fraud model is fooled by small changes to transactions
Adversarial training, validated on held-out attacks
Users try role-play prompts to bypass content policy
Safety training plus input and output classifiers

blocks.title: Targeted mitigation questions
blocks.md: Match the mitigation to the **root cause**: **provenance and data validation** for poisoning, **isolation patterns and least privilege** for prompt injection, **adversarial training** for evasion, **classifiers and safety training** for jailbreaks, and **rate limits and output minimisation** for extraction. Expect the best answers to acknowledge **trade-offs** and to **layer** controls rather than rely on one.

q.q: An agent reads customer emails and can issue refunds. Which mitigation BEST addresses the root cause of prompt injection in this design?
o: A longer system prompt telling the agent to ignore instructions found in emails
Fixing the plan before reading emails, and requiring approval for refunds
A larger model, since bigger models are always better at spotting injection
Logging every email the agent reads, for review at the end of each month
q.why: Plan-then-execute stops email content from changing which actions run, and human approval contains the consequential action. Instructions in prompts are weak, model size isn’t a control, and monthly reviews are too late.

sections.title: Filtering, sandboxing, rate limiting and watermarking

scenes.title: Four everyday controls
scenes.sub: Filtering, sandboxing, rate limiting and watermarking
scenes.say: Four controls turn up in almost every AI mitigation plan: filtering, sandboxing, rate limiting and watermarking. Each is familiar, each needs adapting for AI, and each fails in predictable ways if it is set up carelessly. | This video covers what each control stops, where it sits, and how to tune it.

scenes.title: What each control does
rows: Damage from code and tools that misbehave
Escapes, and permissions that are too broad
scenes.say: Each control does a different job. | Filtering stops or reduces harmful, injected or sensitive content in inputs and outputs. Watch out for evasion, false positives that block legitimate users, and added latency. | Sandboxing contains the damage when code or tools misbehave, whether by accident or because an agent was manipulated. Watch out for escapes, and for sandboxes granted permissions that are too broad. | Rate limiting reduces floods, model extraction and runaway costs. Watch out for attackers spreading requests across many accounts, and for legitimate peaks. | And watermarking marks synthetic content so it can be identified. Watch out for removal and paraphrasing, and remember that detection needs access to the right detector.

scenes.title: Where the controls sit
scenes.say: Here is where the four controls sit. Requests arrive from users, applications and other agents. | A gateway enforces rate limits, quotas and spending budgets per identity, before any expensive work happens. | Input filters check for policy violations, likely injection, and sensitive data. | The model and agent run with least privilege, and any code or tool execution happens inside a sandbox, with no secrets and only allow-listed network access. | Output filters check safety, leakage of sensitive data, and the expected format. | And generated media is marked, with watermarks and content credentials, before it leaves.

items: Filter inputs and outputs; tune and measure both error types
Sandbox code and tools: isolated, ephemeral, no secrets
Rate-limit by identity, tokens and cost, not just requests
Mark synthetic content; watermarks support, not prove
scenes.say: To recap. | Filter both inputs and outputs, and tune filters by measuring both missed attacks and false positives. | Sandbox code and tools: isolated, short-lived, with no secrets. | Rate-limit by identity, tokens and cost, not just by request count. | And mark synthetic content, remembering that watermarks support conclusions rather than prove them.

blocks.md:
### Filtering
- **Where:** on inputs (policy, likely injection, sensitive data) and outputs (safety, data leakage, format and schema), and on content entering retrieval indexes and memory (Module 4.4).
- **How:** rules for known patterns, trained classifiers for harm categories, and model-based judges for nuanced policy, often in combination.
- **Tuning:** set thresholds per category, using labelled adversarial and benign sets. Measure **detection rates and false positive rates**, test in every supported language, and decide in advance whether each filter **fails closed** when unavailable (Module 5.7).
- **Limits:** filters reduce, but don’t eliminate, injection and jailbreaks, so pair them with design-level containment (Section 1).

### Sandboxing
- Run generated code, tool execution and file handling in **isolated environments**, such as microVMs or hardened container runtimes, that are **short-lived** and destroyed after each task.
- Give sandboxes **no secrets**, **least-privilege** access, **allow-listed network egress** and **resource limits** for CPU, memory, time and storage (Module 4.6).
- Treat everything that comes out of a sandbox, including files and results, as untrusted.

### Rate limiting
- Limit by **identity** (user, key, tenant, agent), by **tokens and cost**, not only requests, and by **concurrency** and **agent steps**.
- Set **budgets and hard caps** with alerts, to stop denial-of-wallet and runaway agents (Module 6.1).
- Watch for **probing patterns** that suggest extraction, such as systematic, high-volume queries across the input space, and throttle or challenge them (Module 3.6).

### Watermarking and content marking
- **Watermarks** embed a machine-detectable signal in generated text, images, audio or video; Google’s **SynthID** is one example. **Content credentials** (C2PA) attach signed provenance metadata (Module 2.6).
- Under the **EU AI Act, Article 50**, providers of generative systems must mark synthetic outputs in a machine-readable way. The duty applies from 2 August 2026, with systems already on the market given until 2 December 2026 (Module 2.1).
- **Limits:** marks can be degraded by editing, compression or paraphrasing, especially in text, and detection needs the right detector. Treat a detection result as evidence, not proof, and combine methods.

blocks.title: The filter that cried wolf
blocks.md: After an injection finding, a team deploys a strict input filter on its customer assistant. Attack success in the test suite drops to almost zero. A week later, complaints rise: the filter is blocking 9% of ordinary customer questions, especially those written in Welsh and Polish.

q.q: What should the team do NEXT?
o: Keep the filter as it is, since stopping attacks matters more than complaints
Retune the thresholds using labelled benign and attack sets in every language
Remove the filter completely, and rely on the model’s own safety training
Block all languages other than English, so that the filter performs better
q.why: A filter must be tuned against both error types. Labelled benign and adversarial sets, in every supported language, let the team cut false positives while keeping detection, alongside design-level containment. Ignoring complaints, removing the filter or blocking languages are all poor trade-offs.

blocks.title: Everyday control questions
blocks.md: Filters work on **inputs and outputs**, and must be **tuned on both error types**. Sandboxes are **isolated, short-lived, secret-free and egress-limited**. Rate limits work **per identity, on tokens and cost**, with **budgets and caps**. Watermarks and content credentials **support** provenance claims, but can be removed, so treat detection as **evidence, not proof**.

q.q: A coding agent runs generated code to test it. Which sandbox design is BEST?
o: A long-lived container shared by all users, with the team’s cloud keys for convenience
A short-lived, isolated environment with no secrets and allow-listed network access
The developer’s own laptop, since the developer can watch what the code does
The production server, so tests run in the same environment as live code
q.why: Isolated, ephemeral sandboxes without secrets and with restricted egress contain damage if the code is malicious or the agent is manipulated. The other options expose credentials, people or production.

scenes.title: Which fix first?
scenes.sub: Prioritising mitigations by risk, feasibility and business context
scenes.say: There are always more possible mitigations than time, money and people to build them. Prioritising well means getting the most risk reduction, soonest, without breaking the business. | This video covers how to prioritise mitigations by risk reduction, feasibility and business context.

scenes.title: Risk reduction and effort
scenes.say: Start by placing each candidate mitigation on two axes: how much risk it removes, and how feasible it is. | Large risk reduction and easy to do: these are quick wins, so do them now. | Large risk reduction but hard to do: plan and fund them as strategic work, with interim controls in the meantime. | Small risk reduction and easy: do them when convenient. | And small risk reduction, hard to do: defer or drop them, and record why.

scenes.title: What feasibility really means

items.d: How long the exposure stays open
People who can build and run it

scenes.say: Feasibility has six parts. | Technical fit: does the mitigation work with this architecture, or does it need a redesign? | Cost: not just building it, but running it, including extra compute for classifiers and judges. | Time: how long the exposure stays open while the fix is built. | Skills: whether you have people who can build and operate it. | Vendor dependency: whether it needs a provider to act, on their timetable. | And user impact: friction, false refusals and delays, which can quietly destroy the value of the product.

Useful, but not relied on alone.

scenes.say: Here is a prioritised plan for finding F-07, where injected email text could trigger refunds. It is a plan, not a single fix. | First, an interim control closes the exposure today: the refund tool is switched off for the agent. | The quick win comes next: human approval for every refund, in two days. | Then the strategic fixes address the root cause: isolating email content as data within a week, and redesigning the agent as plan-then-execute over three weeks. | Classifier tuning continues as a supporting control, useful but never relied on alone. | And the residual risk is stated, accepted by the person who owns it, here the CFO, with a review date.

items: Weigh risk reduction against feasibility
Feasibility: fit, cost, time, skills, vendors, user impact
Close exposure now with interim controls
Record decisions; residual risk needs an owner
scenes.say: To recap. | Weigh how much risk each mitigation removes against how feasible it is. | Judge feasibility by technical fit, cost, time, skills, vendor dependency and user impact. | Close the exposure now with interim controls, while strategic fixes are built. | And record every decision, with an owner who accepts the residual risk.

blocks.md:
### Prioritisation factors
| Factor | Questions |
|---|---|
| **Risk reduction** | How much does it lower likelihood or impact for the findings it addresses? Does it fix the root cause or a symptom? Does it cover several findings at once? |
| **Feasibility** | Technical fit, build and running cost (including compute), time to deliver, skills, and dependence on vendors |
| **Business context** | Risk appetite, launch dates, customer and revenue impact, contractual commitments, and the product’s value if the control adds friction |
| **Regulatory drivers** | Deadlines and duties, such as EU AI Act obligations for high-risk or general-purpose AI, or data protection requirements |
| **Side effects** | False refusals, latency, reduced capability, new attack surface |

### Building the plan
- **Interim controls first:** when a serious finding can’t be fixed quickly, contain it now by disabling a tool, adding human approval, narrowing access or tightening limits (Module 5.5).
- **Quick wins, then strategic fixes:** take cheap, high-value steps immediately, and fund root-cause fixes, such as redesigning an agent, as planned work.
- **Layer controls:** avoid relying on a single mitigation, especially a probabilistic one such as a classifier.
- **Group by root cause:** one architectural fix can close many findings, which often makes it the best value even if it is harder.

### Risk treatment and acceptance
Every finding ends in a recorded **treatment decision**, in line with risk management standards such as ISO/IEC 27005 and ISO/IEC 42001: **modify** the risk with mitigations, **avoid** it by not doing the risky thing (for example, removing a capability), **share** it, for example through contracts or insurance, or **retain** it. Retained and residual risk must be **accepted by an owner with the authority to do so**, within the risk appetite, and given a **review date** (Module 2.3). If the residual risk exceeds the appetite and no interim control exists, the right answer may be **not to launch**.

blocks.title: The four-month fix
blocks.md: A red team finds that a customer-facing agent can be steered into revealing other customers’ order histories. The root-cause fix, rebuilding retrieval with per-user permissions, will take four months. Launch is planned for next week, and the product director wants to launch on time and fix it later.

q.q: What is the BEST way forward?
o: Launch on time, and schedule the four-month fix for after the launch
Apply interim controls that close the exposure now, then fund the full fix
Cancel the product, since no AI system can ever be fully secured anyway
Launch on time, but add a disclaimer telling customers not to ask for data
q.why: Exposing customers’ data is outside any reasonable risk appetite, so the exposure must be closed before launch, for example by removing order history from the agent’s reach until per-user permissions exist. The root-cause fix then follows as planned work. Launching exposed, cancelling outright or relying on a disclaimer are all poor choices.

blocks.title: Prioritisation questions
blocks.md: The best answers **contain serious exposure immediately** with interim controls, take **quick wins** next, and **plan root-cause fixes**, weighing **risk reduction against feasibility and business context**. Residual risk is **accepted by an accountable owner** within appetite, with a review date. "Launch now, fix later" for a serious, exploitable flaw is a trap.

q.q: Two mitigations are proposed for the same risk: a classifier that blocks 80% of attacks, live in a day, and an architectural change that removes the attack path, live in six weeks. What is the BEST plan?
o: Deploy the classifier only, since 80% protection arriving in a day is good enough
Deploy the classifier now as an interim layer, and build the architectural fix
Build only the architectural fix, leaving the system exposed for six weeks
Do neither, since the two options can’t both be afforded within the budget
q.why: Layering a quick interim control with the root-cause fix reduces risk immediately and removes the attack path later. Relying on the classifier alone leaves residual risk, and waiting six weeks leaves the system exposed.

blocks.title: Prove the fix works, and keeps working

scenes.title: Prove the fix works, and keeps working
scenes.say: A mitigation isn’t finished when it is deployed. It is finished when testing shows it works, without breaking the product, and when tests will catch it if it stops working. With AI, things stop working more often than you might think. | This video covers validating mitigations through regression testing.

scenes.title: From finding to regression test
scenes.say: Every confirmed finding becomes a regression test. It starts from the finding’s reproduction package. | The test case repeats the original conditions, many times, so it measures a success rate. | Variants test whether the fix generalises, rather than just blocking the exact input that was reported. Keep some variants out of any tuning, so they stay a fair test. | A benign set of normal requests checks that the fix hasn’t broken legitimate use. | The whole suite runs after every change: model updates, prompt edits, guardrail changes and new tools. | And a release gate blocks any change that pushes a result past its threshold.

scenes.title: A regression caught by the gate
scenes.yLabel: Illustrative results for the F-07 test suite
scenes.say: Here is the suite at work. Before the fix, in release one, the attack succeeded thirty-one per cent of the time. The fix in release two brought it down to two per cent. Then a provider model update in release three pushed it back up to nine per cent. | The release gate is set at five per cent, so release three was blocked automatically, before customers saw it, and the team re-tuned the mitigation for release four. | Meanwhile, refusals of ordinary requests stayed close to one per cent, so the fix protected users without getting in their way.

scenes.title: Two questions for every fix
rows: Attack success on cases and variants
scenes.say: Every fix must answer two questions. | Does it stop attacks? Measure attack success on the original cases and their variants. Does it break things? Measure task quality and false refusals. | It passes on security when attack success falls below the agreed threshold. It passes on utility when quality shows no meaningful drop from the baseline. | And watch for the classic failures: a fix that only blocks the exact input that was reported, and a product that slowly gets worse with every extra layer of protection.

items: Turn every finding into a regression test
Test variants and benign requests, many times
Run the suite after every change, behind a release gate
Retest independently before closing serious findings
scenes.say: To recap. | Turn every confirmed finding into a regression test. | Test variants and benign requests, many times each. | Run the suite after every change, behind a release gate. | And for serious findings, have the red team retest independently before closing them.

blocks.md:
### Building regression suites from findings
- **Start from the reproduction package** (Module 6.5): the same versions, settings and inputs, repeated enough times to measure a success rate.
- **Add variants:** rephrasings, other languages and formats, multi-turn versions and different entry points, generated by people or attacker models (Module 6.4). Keep a **held-out set** that is never used to tune prompts, classifiers or training, so the suite stays an honest test.
- **Add benign baselines:** representative legitimate requests, including edge cases, to catch over-blocking and quality loss.
- **Use enough trials:** small samples hide differences. Decide the number of runs and the pass thresholds in advance.

### When to run the suite
Run it on **every behaviour-changing change**: model and provider updates, fine-tuning, prompt and template edits, retrieval index or embedding changes, guardrail and threshold changes, new tools or permissions, and dependency upgrades (Module 6.2). Provider-side updates can arrive without notice, so also run it **on a schedule** against production-equivalent settings.

### Release gates and closure
- **Gate releases** in the pipeline: a change that pushes any security or utility result past its threshold doesn’t ship without an approved exception (Module 6.2).
- **Independent retest:** for serious findings, the red team, not the builders, confirms the fix before closure, including attempts to bypass it.
- **Record results** against the finding, and keep trend data: rising attack success across releases is an early warning (Section 5).

### Common validation mistakes
- Testing only the exact input from the report, so the fix is **overfitted** to one string.
- Tuning on the test set, which **contaminates** it and inflates results.
- Declaring success from **one run** of a non-deterministic system.
- Ignoring **utility**: a fix that makes the product unusable will be switched off, which reintroduces the risk.

blocks.title: Validating a fix for an injection finding
items: Reproduce the baseline
Run the original case and its variants on the current release to confirm the attack success rate before the fix.
Apply the mitigation
Deploy the fix to staging through the pipeline, with the release manifest updated.
Re-run security tests
Run original cases, variants and held-out variants many times, and compare rates against the threshold.
Re-run utility tests
Run the benign set and quality evaluations, and compare with the baseline.
Retest independently and gate
Have the red team attempt bypasses, then add the cases to the release gate and close the finding.

blocks.title: Validation questions
blocks.md: A fix is validated when **repeated tests** show attack success **below threshold on the original case and on held-out variants**, **utility is preserved**, and the cases are **in a regression suite** that runs on every change behind a **release gate**. One clean run, or a fix that only blocks the reported input, isn’t validation.

q.q: After a fix, the exact prompt from a red team report no longer works, but testers haven’t tried any variants. Why is the finding NOT ready to close?
o: Findings can only be closed by the vendor of the underlying model
The fix may only block the reported input, not the underlying weakness
Every finding must stay open for at least ninety days after its fix
The red team must first publish the original prompt for peer review
q.why: Without variants, including held-out ones, there is no evidence the fix addresses the weakness rather than one string. Repeated tests on variants, plus utility checks, are needed before closure.

scenes.title: The risk that remains
scenes.say: After every mitigation, some risk remains. With AI, that residual risk doesn’t stay still: models are updated, attackers publish new techniques, and agents gain new tools. Risk that was acceptable last quarter may not be acceptable today. | This video covers continuous monitoring for residual risk.

scenes.title: Signals of residual risk

items.d: Automated red teaming on a timer

scenes.say: Six kinds of signal show how residual risk is moving. | Guardrail activity: block rates and near misses, and sudden changes in either. | Attack attempts: detections and suspicious patterns in logs, as Domain 5 described. | Scheduled testing: automated red teaming that reruns the regression suite and new techniques on a timer. | Production canaries: honeytokens and canary records that should never appear in an output or a request. If one fires, something is wrong. | Threat intelligence: newly published techniques, and incidents at other organisations. | And user reports, from in-product feedback to bug bounty submissions.

scenes.title: The residual risk loop
scenes.intro: Accepted risk is reviewed, not forgotten.
scenes.say: Residual risk moves through a loop. | Accept: an owner with authority signs off the remaining risk, within the risk appetite. | Monitor: key risk indicators track it, such as attack success in scheduled tests. | Detect change: thresholds and triggers flag when an indicator moves, or when something changes, such as a model update or a new tool. | Reassess: re-test, and re-rate the risk. | Treat: add or tune mitigations if the risk has grown. | And review on a schedule, even when everything looks quiet, because acceptance should expire rather than last forever.

scenes.title: Residual risk that grew

events.d: Injection risk at 2% in tests, signed off

scenes.say: Here is residual risk that grew, and was caught. | In month zero, an injection risk is accepted at a two per cent success rate in testing, with an owner and a review date. | In month two, researchers publish a new multi-turn technique. | Three days later, the scheduled tests include it, and attack success jumps to eleven per cent, breaching the key risk indicator threshold. | Within a week, the team adds a new mitigation, and new cases join the regression suite. | By month three, the rate is back to one and a half per cent, and the owner renews the acceptance. Without monitoring, the eleven per cent would have been found by an attacker instead.

items: Residual risk changes as models, tools and attackers change
Watch guardrails, attacks, scheduled tests, canaries, intel, reports
Set KRIs with thresholds and triggers for reassessment
Acceptance has an owner and an expiry date
scenes.say: To recap. | Residual risk changes as models, tools and attackers change. | Watch guardrail activity, attack attempts, scheduled tests, production canaries, threat intelligence and user reports. | Set key risk indicators with thresholds, and triggers that force reassessment. | And make sure every acceptance has an owner, and an expiry date.

blocks.md:
### Residual risk
**Residual risk** is the risk left after mitigations (Module 2.3). It is recorded in the risk register with its owner, the rationale for accepting it, the controls it depends on, and a review date. For AI, residual risk drifts because the system and the threat landscape keep changing.

### Key risk indicators
| Indicator | Example threshold | Action when breached |
|---|---|---|
| **Attack success in scheduled tests** | Above 5% for any high-severity category | Reassess; treat; gate releases |
| **Guardrail block rate** | Doubles week on week, or falls sharply after an update | Investigate an attack campaign or a broken filter |
| **Canary or honeytoken hits** | Any hit | Treat as a potential incident (Module 5.5) |
| **Agent action anomalies** | Tool calls far above baseline | Throttle or pause the agent (Module 5.7) |
| **False refusal rate** | Above the agreed level | Retune, so the control isn’t switched off |
| **Open findings past deadline** | Any P1 past its date | Escalate to the risk owner |

### Triggers for reassessment
- **Changes:** model or provider updates, fine-tuning, new tools, data sources or permissions, and major prompt or guardrail changes (Module 6.2).
- **Threats:** new techniques, new ATLAS case studies, and incidents involving similar systems (Module 6.1).
- **Signals:** a breached indicator, a canary hit, or a credible user or bug bounty report.
- **Time:** scheduled reviews, even when all is quiet; acceptance should expire, not roll over silently.

### Continuous validation
- Run **automated red teaming on a schedule** in a production-equivalent environment, including new techniques as they are published (Module 6.4).
- Place **canaries and honeytokens** in production data, prompts and tools, so misuse reveals itself.
- Feed confirmed issues back into the **regression suite** and the **threat model**, closing the loop between monitoring, testing and mitigation.
- Report residual risk trends to leadership alongside other key risks, in the same language and scales (Module 6.5).

blocks.title: Signal and response
pairs: A canary customer record appears in an assistant’s output
Treat as a potential incident and investigate
A new jailbreak technique is published by researchers
Add it to scheduled tests and reassess the risk
Guardrail block rates fall sharply after a provider update
Check whether the filter still works
An accepted risk reaches its review date with no incidents
Review and renew, adjust or close it
False refusals climb after a new safety control
Retune, so that the control isn’t abandoned

blocks.title: Residual risk questions
blocks.md: Residual risk is **owned, accepted within appetite, monitored and reviewed**. Expect the best answers to use **key risk indicators with thresholds**, **scheduled automated testing**, **canaries**, and **triggers** such as model updates or newly published techniques. "Accepted once, never revisited" is a trap.

q.q: An organisation accepted a residual prompt injection risk six months ago. Since then, the model provider has updated the model twice and the agent has gained two new tools. What should happen?
o: Nothing, because the risk was formally accepted by its owner six months ago
Reassess: re-run the tests on the current system, re-rate it, renew or treat
Remove the two new tools, since adding tools always invalidates acceptance
Ask the provider to confirm that its updates didn’t affect the risk level
q.why: Model updates and new tools are triggers for reassessment. Re-testing the current system shows whether the accepted risk still holds, so the owner can renew, adjust or treat it.

sections.title: Deep dive: robustness defences and guardrail models

scenes.title: Hardening models and guarding them
scenes.sub: Adversarial training, certified robustness and guardrail models
scenes.say: Section one matched each attack class to a targeted mitigation. This deep dive looks inside two of the most important: making the model itself more robust, and wrapping it in separate guardrail models that check what goes in and what comes out. | For each, you will see what it really guarantees, what it costs, and how to evaluate it.

scenes.title: Empirical or certified robustness?
rows: A proof within a set radius
Holds against any attack in range
A new attack may still break it
scenes.say: Robustness comes in two kinds. | Empirical robustness is shown by surviving the strongest known attacks. Certified robustness is proved mathematically, for any change within a set radius. | The main empirical method is adversarial training with PGD, and variants such as TRADES. Certified methods include randomised smoothing and formal verifiers. | Empirical methods scale to large, practical models. A certificate holds against any attack within its range, including attacks not yet invented. | But an empirical defence can fall to a new attack, while certificates cover only small radii, cost more to compute, and sometimes abstain rather than answer.

scenes.title: Randomised smoothing: a provable answer, or none
scenes.say: Randomised smoothing, introduced by Cohen and colleagues in 2019, turns an ordinary classifier into one with a provable guarantee. It starts with the input to be classified. | It makes many copies of the input, each with random Gaussian noise added. | The ordinary, base classifier labels every noisy copy. | The votes are counted, and the smoothed classifier returns the most common label. | If that label wins clearly, the answer comes with a certificate: no change within a radius R, measured in the L-two norm, can alter it. More noise gives larger radii, but lower accuracy. | If the vote is too close to call, the classifier abstains rather than guessing, so the system needs a fallback, such as human review.

scenes.title: Guardrail models and services
scenes.say: Guardrail models are separate classifiers that check what goes into and comes out of the main model. Here are eight you may meet. | Meta’s Llama Guard is an open-weight model that labels prompts and responses against a hazard taxonomy. Version four also handles images. | Llama Prompt Guard two is a small, fast classifier that flags prompt injection and jailbreak attempts. | Google’s ShieldGemma models judge content against a written safety policy. | Microsoft’s Prompt Shields, in Azure AI Content Safety, detect attacks both in user prompts and in documents the model reads. | NVIDIA’s NeMo Guardrails is an open-source toolkit for programmable rails on inputs, dialogue, retrieval and outputs. | Guardrails AI is an open-source framework of validators that check and correct model outputs. | Amazon Bedrock Guardrails combines content and prompt-attack filters, denied topics, personal data filters and grounding checks. | And Anthropic’s Constitutional Classifiers are trained on synthetic data generated from a set of principles. A twenty twenty-six update cut their extra compute to about one per cent.

scenes.title: A guardrail stack, defence in depth

layers.label: Input checks
layers.sub: injection and jailbreak detection; personal data redaction

layers.label: Context controls
layers.sub: retrieval permissions, tool allowlists, least privilege

layers.label: Output checks
layers.sub: harm classifiers, grounding and data leakage checks

scenes.say: No single guardrail is enough, so they are stacked. | Input checks screen prompts and documents for injection and jailbreak attempts, and redact personal data. | Context controls limit what the model can reach: retrieval permissions, tool allowlists and least privilege, which still work when a classifier misses. | The model’s own safety training is the middle layer. | Output checks catch harmful content, ungrounded claims and data leakage before anything reaches a user or a tool. | And monitoring watches whole conversations and the rates of blocks and alerts, to catch slow, multi-turn attacks and drift.

items: Adversarial training resists known attacks, at a cost
Certificates prove robustness, but only within a radius
Guardrail models check inputs and outputs independently
Test guardrails for misses, false blocks and evasion
scenes.say: To recap. | Adversarial training makes a model resist the attacks it was trained against, at a cost in compute and clean accuracy. | Certified methods prove robustness, but only within a small radius, and may abstain. | Guardrail models check inputs and outputs independently of the main model. | And every guardrail must be tested for misses, for false blocks of legitimate use, and for deliberate evasion.

blocks.md:
### Adversarial training in practice
**PGD adversarial training** (Madry et al., 2018) generates adversarial examples on the fly and trains on them at every step. Know its costs and limits:
- **Compute:** each training step runs several attack iterations, so training costs several times more. Cheaper single-step variants must be watched for **catastrophic overfitting**, where robustness suddenly collapses.
- **Accuracy:** clean accuracy usually falls. **TRADES** (Zhang et al., 2019) makes the trade-off between clean accuracy and robustness an explicit, tunable term.
- **Scope:** robustness holds mainly for the threat model used in training, such as L∞ at 8/255, not for other norms, patches or new kinds of attack.
- **Robust overfitting:** robust accuracy on test data can peak and then decline during training, so stop early using a robust validation set.

For language models, the equivalent is safety training on red-team data, including optimised attacks, combined with classifiers.

### Certified robustness
- **Randomised smoothing** (Cohen, Rosenfeld and Kolter, 2019) classifies many Gaussian-noised copies of an input and returns the majority label, with a certified L2 radius that grows with the noise level and the winning margin. It abstains when the vote is too close.
- **Bound propagation and formal verification** prove that no input within a region can change the output, but scale poorly to large models.

Certificates cover a stated norm and radius only, usually smaller than the changes attackers can make in practice. They are most valuable for smaller, high-stakes models where a provable bound matters.

### Guardrail models and services
| Tool | Provider | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Llama Guard 3 and 4** | Meta | Open-weight classifiers that label prompts and responses against the MLCommons hazard taxonomy; version 4 (12B) also handles images |
| **Llama Prompt Guard 2** | Meta | Small classifiers (86M and 22M parameters) that flag prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, with a 512-token window |
| **ShieldGemma** | Google | Open-weight safety classifiers that judge content against a written policy |
| **Prompt Shields** | Microsoft Azure | Detects attacks in user prompts and in documents the model processes |
| **NeMo Guardrails** | NVIDIA | Open-source toolkit for programmable input, dialogue, retrieval and output rails, written in Colang |
| **Guardrails AI** | Open source | Validators that check and correct outputs for format, personal data, toxicity and more |
| **Bedrock Guardrails** | AWS | Content and prompt-attack filters, denied topics, personal data filters and contextual grounding checks |
| **Constitutional Classifiers** | Anthropic | Input and output classifiers trained on synthetic data generated from a constitution (Section 1). A 2026 version screens traffic with a cheap probe of the model’s internal activations, escalating flagged exchanges, for about 1% extra compute |

### Evaluating a guardrail
- **Misses and false blocks:** measure detection on your own attack sets, and false positives on realistic benign traffic, in every language you support.
- **Evasion:** Hackett and colleagues (2025) evaded six prompt injection and jailbreak detectors, including Azure Prompt Shield and Meta’s Prompt Guard, using character injection and adversarial machine learning techniques, in some cases with up to 100% success. Test obfuscated variants, not just known attacks.
- **Coverage:** check context limits (long inputs may need splitting), every modality, and whether indirect content such as retrieved documents and tool results is screened.
- **Operations:** latency, cost, whether failures block or allow traffic (fail closed or fail open), and logging for monitoring (Section 5).

A guardrail is one layer. Pair it with least privilege, sandboxing and human approval for high-impact actions, which still protect the system when a classifier misses.

blocks.title: Robustness and guardrail terms
cards: Resistance shown by surviving the strongest known attacks; a new attack may still break it.
A mathematical guarantee that no change within a stated radius can alter the output.
Classifying many noisy copies of an input and returning the majority label, with a certified radius or an abstention.
An adversarial training method that tunes the trade-off between clean accuracy and robustness.
A separate classifier that screens a model’s inputs or outputs against a safety or security policy.
When a guardrail errors or times out, traffic is blocked rather than allowed through.

blocks.title: Evaluating a guardrail before relying on it
items: Build the test sets
Assemble attack prompts for each family in Module 6.4, plus a realistic benign set from your own traffic.
Measure both errors
Record the detection rate on attacks and the false positive rate on benign inputs, per language and channel.
Try to evade it
Test obfuscated, encoded and character-level variants, and indirect content such as documents and tool results.
Check the operations
Measure latency and cost, confirm the failure mode, and make sure decisions are logged for monitoring.
Layer and retest
Keep least privilege and approvals behind the guardrail, and rerun the tests whenever either side changes.

q.q: A medical imaging model is protected by randomised smoothing. On some scans, it returns no diagnosis at all. What is the MOST likely explanation?
o: The base classifier has failed and must be retrained before further use
The noisy votes were too close to call, so the classifier abstained
An attacker has disabled the model through a denial of service attack
The certified radius was set to zero, disabling all predictions
q.why: Randomised smoothing abstains when the most common label among noisy copies doesn’t win by a clear margin. That is designed behaviour, so the system needs a fallback such as human review, not evidence of failure or attack.

quiz.q: Which mitigation targets the root cause of training data poisoning?
o: Rate limiting the model’s public API by user and by token count
Provenance tracking and data validation before training
Watermarking every output that the model generates
Adding a disclaimer to the application’s user interface
quiz.why: Poisoning enters through data, so verifying where data comes from and validating it before training addresses the root cause.

quiz.q: What is a known limitation of adversarial training?
o: It can only be used on models that have fewer than a million parameters
It hardens models against attacks seen, but new techniques can still succeed
It permanently removes the need for any input or output filtering at all
It makes models completely immune to every possible kind of evasion attack
quiz.why: Adversarial training improves robustness to known attacks, often at some cost to accuracy, and needs repeating as attackers adapt.

quiz.q: What is the core principle behind design patterns that contain prompt injection?
o: Every agent should use the largest and most capable model available
Once untrusted input is read, it mustn’t trigger consequential actions
Agents should be given broad tools, so that they can recover from attacks
System prompts should be kept secret, so attackers can’t learn their rules
quiz.why: Patterns such as plan-then-execute and dual LLM constrain agents so that untrusted content can’t change which consequential actions run.

quiz.q: Why should a content filter be tuned using both adversarial and benign test sets?
o: Benign sets are needed to make the filter run faster in production
To measure missed attacks and false positives, and balance the two
Because regulators require equal numbers of each kind of test
Adversarial sets alone are too expensive to create in most cases
quiz.why: A filter that blocks attacks but also blocks many legitimate requests may be switched off; both error types must be measured.

quiz.q: Which practice BEST describes a well-designed code execution sandbox?
o: Long-lived, shared by every user, with cloud keys for convenience
Isolated, short-lived, with no secrets and allow-listed egress
Running inside the production database server, for speed
Open network access, so code can install anything it needs
quiz.why: Isolation, short life, no secrets and restricted egress contain the damage if executed code is malicious or an agent is manipulated.

quiz.q: Why should AI rate limits consider tokens and cost, not just request counts?
o: Request counts are impossible to measure accurately at an API gateway
Just a few very long requests can consume huge resources and money
Token limits are required for every AI system under the EU AI Act
Cost-based limits make every individual response noticeably faster
quiz.why: One request can carry an enormous prompt or trigger a long agent loop, so limits on tokens, cost and steps prevent floods and denial of wallet.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an interim control?
o: To replace the permanent fix, so that it never needs to be built
To contain a risk now, while the full fix is still being built
To document a risk for auditors without changing anything
To transfer all responsibility for the risk to the vendor
quiz.why: Interim controls, such as disabling a tool or adding approval, close the exposure immediately while strategic fixes are delivered.

quiz.q: Which is a risk treatment option in standards such as ISO/IEC 27005?
o: Ignore the risk, until an incident proves that it was real
Avoid the risk, for example by removing the risky capability
Hide the risk from the board, to avoid causing any alarm
Delay all decisions until the next annual risk review
quiz.why: Risks can be modified, avoided, shared or retained; avoidance means not doing the risky activity at all.

quiz.q: Why should a regression suite include variants of a reported attack?
o: Variants make the suite take longer to run, which gives better coverage
To check the fix addresses the weakness, not just the reported input
Variants are needed so that the report looks more thorough to readers
Because the original reported input is usually impossible to rerun
quiz.why: A fix that only blocks one string is overfitted. Variants, including held-out ones, show whether it generalises.

quiz.q: What does a release gate do in a regression testing pipeline?
o: It lets anyone deploy a change without running any tests first
It blocks changes that push results past agreed thresholds
It records test results only after a release has gone live
It replaces the need for an independent retest by the red team
quiz.why: A gate stops a change from shipping when security or utility results cross their thresholds, unless an exception is approved.

quiz.q: Why must benign requests be part of mitigation validation?
o: Benign requests are the easiest test cases for any team to write quickly
A fix that breaks normal use may be switched off, bringing back the risk
Regulators require benign tests before any AI system is allowed to launch
Benign requests reveal new attack techniques faster than red teams
quiz.why: Utility matters: over-blocking frustrates users and creates pressure to remove the control, reintroducing the risk.

quiz.q: Which event should trigger reassessment of an accepted residual AI risk?
o: A routine change to the colour scheme of the user interface
A provider model update, or a new tool given to the agent
A new employee joining the marketing department
A scheduled office move to another floor of the building
quiz.why: Model updates and new capabilities change behaviour and exposure, so accepted risks must be re-tested and re-rated.

quiz.q: What should happen when a production canary record appears in an AI output?
o: Delete the canary record, so it can’t appear in any more outputs
Treat it as a potential incident, and investigate how it leaked
Ignore it, because canary records are only used during testing
Raise the guardrail threshold, so that fewer outputs are checked
quiz.why: Canaries should never appear in normal use, so a hit signals possible misuse or leakage that needs investigation.

quiz.q: What is a key limitation of PGD adversarial training?
o: It can only be applied to models with fewer than a billion parameters
Robustness mainly covers the attack type and budget used in training
It removes the need to test the model with new attacks after release
It improves clean accuracy so much that robustness becomes unnecessary
quiz.why: Adversarial training hardens a model against the threat model it trained on, such as one norm and budget. Other norms, patches and new attack types can still succeed, and clean accuracy usually falls.

quiz.q: What does a certificate from randomised smoothing guarantee?
o: No change an attacker could make, however large, can alter it
No change within a stated L2 radius can alter that input’s label
Every input from the training distribution is classified correctly
Gradient-based attacks fail, though black-box attacks may succeed
quiz.why: Randomised smoothing certifies, for a specific input, that no perturbation within a stated L2 radius can change the smoothed classifier’s output. It says nothing about larger changes or overall accuracy.

quiz.q: A team adds an open-weight guardrail model that screens prompts for jailbreak attempts. Which evaluation is MOST important before relying on it?
o: Confirm the guardrail model is larger than the main model it protects
Measure missed attacks, false blocks and evasion with obfuscated inputs
Check that the guardrail’s developer is certified under ISO/IEC 27001
Verify that it blocks every prompt containing suspicious keywords
quiz.why: A guardrail has to be measured on your own traffic for misses and false positives, and tested against deliberate evasion, which research shows can defeat detectors. Size, certification and keyword blocking don’t show it works.

quiz.q: A small prompt injection classifier has a 512-token context window, but the application accepts documents of up to 20,000 tokens. What should the design do?
o: Scan only the first 512 tokens, since attacks usually appear at the start
Split long inputs into segments and scan each, alongside other controls
Remove the classifier, since it can’t process complete documents
Raise the classifier’s threshold, so it flags less of each document
quiz.why: Content beyond the window would go unscanned, and attackers can place instructions anywhere. Splitting inputs into segments and scanning each, as Meta recommends for Prompt Guard 2, keeps coverage, with other controls behind it.

exam.q: A bank’s fraud model is being evaded by small, deliberate changes to transaction features. Which mitigation BEST targets this threat?
o: Watermarking the model’s outputs, so evasion attempts can be traced back
Adversarial training on such changes, validated against held-out attacks
Adding a longer system prompt telling the model to watch for manipulation
Increasing the API rate limit, so the model can process more transactions
exam.why: Adversarial training targets evasion directly, and validating it on held-out attacks checks it generalises. Watermarks, prompts and rate limits don’t address evasion of a fraud model.

exam.q: A research assistant agent reads web pages and can send emails. Testing shows injected page text can make it email confidential notes. Which change addresses the root cause MOST effectively?
o: Adding a filter that looks for suspicious phrases in each web page
Redesigning so web content can’t change actions, with approval for emails
Asking users not to research any topics on unfamiliar or untrusted websites
Switching to a different model provider with stronger safety training
exam.why: Containing untrusted content by design, for example plan-then-execute or a quarantined reader, with approval for consequential actions, removes the attack path. Filters, user advice and model changes only reduce it.

exam.q: After a new output filter is deployed, the help desk reports that the assistant now refuses many legitimate questions about medication doses from pharmacists. What should the security team do FIRST?
o: Remove the filter immediately, since user satisfaction is the priority
Measure false positives on labelled benign sets, and retune for this use
Tell the pharmacists to rephrase their questions to avoid the filter
Keep the filter unchanged, since some over-blocking is always acceptable
exam.why: Measuring false positives with labelled benign data, then retuning thresholds or adding context-aware rules, keeps protection while restoring utility. Removing, ignoring or working around the filter are poor responses.

exam.q: A provider’s API is being queried systematically by a small number of accounts in what looks like a model extraction attempt. Which response is BEST?
o: Publish the model’s weights, since extraction is now inevitable anyway
Throttle those accounts, minimise output detail, and investigate them
Double the rate limits for all users, to keep the service responsive
Watermark all outputs, and take no other action against the accounts
exam.why: Per-identity throttling, returning less detail and investigating raise the cost of extraction and confirm intent. Watermarks help prove theft later but don’t stop it.

exam.q: A serious finding has two fixes: an approval step that takes two days to add, and a redesign that takes two months. The product launches in a week. What is the BEST plan?
o: Launch, and start the two-month redesign immediately after the launch
Add the approval step before launch, and fund the redesign as planned work
Delay the launch by two months, until the redesign is fully complete
Launch, and add the approval step if an incident occurs afterwards
exam.why: The quick win reduces risk before launch, and the redesign addresses the root cause later. Delaying two months may be disproportionate if the interim control brings risk within appetite.

exam.q: A residual risk remains after mitigation, and a team lead informally agrees to "live with it". What is MISSING from good practice?
o: Nothing, since any team lead can accept risks of any size on their own
Acceptance by an owner with authority, within appetite, with a review date
A press release explaining the risk to the organisation’s customers
An immediate decision to stop using AI anywhere in that business process
exam.why: Residual risk must be formally accepted by someone with authority, within the risk appetite, recorded in the register and reviewed.

exam.q: A fix for an injection finding blocks the exact prompt from the report. Testers then find that a translated version of the same attack still works. What does this show?
o: The fix works, since translated attacks are always out of scope for testing
The fix is overfitted; validate with variants, including held-out ones
Translation tools should be blocked for every user of the system
The original finding was a false positive, and can now be closed
exam.why: A fix that fails on simple variants addresses the string, not the weakness. Validation needs variants across languages, formats and turns, including held-out cases.

exam.q: A team tunes its injection classifier until it scores perfectly on the regression suite, using the suite’s own cases as tuning data. Why is the perfect score unreliable?
o: Perfect scores are always caused by a software bug in the harness
The suite has been contaminated, so it no longer tests generalisation
Classifiers can never be tuned without the model provider’s consent
Regression suites must be rebuilt from scratch for every release
exam.why: Tuning on test cases inflates results. Held-out variants that are never used for tuning keep the suite an honest measure.

exam.q: Scheduled automated red teaming shows attack success on a key category rising from 2% to 11% after a newly published technique was added to the tests. What should happen NEXT?
o: Remove the new technique from the tests, so the results return to normal
Treat it as a breached KRI: reassess, mitigate and add regression cases
Wait for the next annual review to discuss the change in results
Accept the new level, since accepted risks can’t be reopened
exam.why: A breached key risk indicator triggers reassessment and treatment, with new cases added to the regression suite, so the risk returns within appetite.

exam.q: Which approach BEST maintains confidence in an AI system’s residual risk between formal assessments?
o: Relying on the most recent penetration test report until the next one
KRIs, scheduled testing, canaries and triggered reassessments
Asking users to report problems, with no other monitoring
Freezing the system, so that its risk can never change again
exam.why: Continuous signals, scheduled testing and triggers keep residual risk visible as models, tools and threats change. Point-in-time reports go stale, and freezing the system is rarely practical.

exam.q: An organisation relies on a single guardrail model to block prompt injection for an agent that can make payments. Testing shows character-level obfuscation evades the guardrail 40% of the time. What is the BEST course of action?
o: Replace the guardrail with a larger model from a different vendor
Keep the guardrail, and add least privilege and approval for payments
Accept the risk, since 60% of obfuscated attacks are still blocked
Remove the guardrail, since it gives a false sense of security
exam.why: Guardrails can be evaded, so high-impact actions need controls that hold when a classifier misses: least privilege and human approval. A larger model may be evaded too, and removing a working layer weakens defence in depth.

exam.q: A guardrail service sometimes times out under heavy load. For an agent that can change customer records, what should happen to requests when the guardrail times out?
o: Fail open: let requests through so customers aren’t delayed
Fail closed: hold or block requests until the check completes
Send requests to the model unchecked, but log them for review
Retry once, then let the request through if it times out again
exam.why: For an agent with write access to customer records, an unchecked request can cause real harm, so the safe failure mode is to hold or block until the check succeeds. Failing open hands attackers a way round the control: overload it.

exam.q: A hospital must choose between an imaging model with empirical robustness from adversarial training and a smoothed model certified against small changes, which sometimes abstains. It needs provable assurance and has radiologists available. Which option fits BEST?
o: The empirical model, since adversarial training is a mathematical proof
The certified model, with abstentions routed to radiologist review
The certified model, with abstentions treated as negative results
The empirical model, since certified models can’t be used in healthcare
exam.why: Only the certified model provides provable assurance within its radius, and its abstentions need a safe fallback such as specialist review. Treating abstentions as negative results could miss disease.
